title: Redundant Input Sequence Consolidation for Cross-Request Key-Value Sharing
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Our serving runtime stores per-request key-value (KV) cache entries for input token sequences. Many customer workloads submit semantically identical or near-identical leading input sequences (system prompts, templates, assistant instructions) which are being cached separately because of small surface differences (whitespace, variable placeholders, tokenization artifacts). This multiplies GPU memory usage and increases eviction churn under load.
goals: 1) Detect and consolidate redundant input sequences across concurrent and sequential requests without changing model outputs. 2) Reduce live KV footprint across GPUs and lower eviction-induced recomputation. 3) Preserve latency SLOs (p50 < 80ms for short requests) and avoid introducing blocking synchronization points during continuous batching.
acceptance_criteria: 1) End-to-end median GPU KV memory per-worker reduced by >= 8% on mixed PLG workloads. 2) End-to-end tail latency (p95) does not regress more than 5% on existing benchmarks. 3) No user-visible change to generation for canonicalized sequences. 4) Feature gated behind runtime flag and rolloutable per-customer.
design_notes: Approach: build a lightweight dedupe layer that computes a canonical signature for the leading token sequence of a request and enables shared KV references for identical signatures. Key points: - Use stable tokenizer-normalized hashing: normalize unicode, strip non-semantic whitespace, substitute common placeholder tokens with a canonical marker, then compute a 64-bit fingerprint. - Store a small reference table on each GPU worker that maps signature -> canonical KV handle. - Reference counting for shared KV frames to manage eviction safely. - During continuous batching, the scheduler can place requests with identical signatures into the same KV reuse bucket without waiting for full batch alignment. - Avoid cross-GPU synchronization by only sharing within a worker's local shard; orchestrator routing will prefer the same worker for warm paths when policy allows.
tradeoffs: - Conservative canonicalization avoids aggressive normalization to prevent semantic changes, which means some near-duplicates will still miss and remain unshared. - Local-only sharing avoids cross-GPU locking but reduces maximum reuse for multi-shard models. - Storing extra small signature index consumes CPU memory and some GPU pinned memory, but lowers overall KV allocations. - Reference counting complexity interacts with eviction and preemption; we add lightweight epoch IDs to detect stale reuse.
implementation_plan: 1) Prototype signature function in Python tokenization shim (perf tests). 2) Implement C++ runtime signer and in-memory signature table on worker. 3) Integrate reference-counted KV handle with existing slab allocator. 4) Add scheduler hint that prefers local reuse when signature exists. 5) Add telemetry (reuse hit rate, avg refcount, memory delta) and rollout flag. 6) Gradual rollout: internal traffic -> beta customers -> GA.
tasks: RUNTIME: add signature table and APIs in worker process
ALLOCATOR: wire reference counting into slab allocator
SCHEDULER: batch-hint integration for reuse buckets
TESTS: deterministic correctness tests for canonicalized vs raw inputs
BENCH: run mixed PLG benchmark (templates + chat) and collect memory/latency metrics
TELEMETRY: reuse-hit-rate, per-worker memory delta, refcount distribution

2026-03-08 - Marco Hernandez: Implemented signature table in worker (WIP). Measuring overhead: signature map uses ~1.2MB per worker for 50k signatures; acceptable. Added epoch ID to detect stale references after compaction.

2026-03-12 - Security: Reviewed. No PII retention changes; canonicalization runs on token ids only. No additional security review required.
2026-03-13 - Marco Hernandez: Opened PR for slab allocator refcount wiring. Need design review: eviction should decrement refs asynchronously to avoid blocking insert hot-paths.
